Database Management Systems: ACID Transactions and Concurrency Control A transaction in a database management system is a logical unit of database processing that includes one or more database access operations. Transactions must satisfy the ACID properties: 1. Atomicity: Either all operations of the transaction are executed and reflected in the database, or none are. Handled by the write-ahead logging (WAL) recovery manager. 2. Consistency: Execution of a transaction in isolation preserves database consistency invariants and integrity constraints. 3. Isolation: Even if multiple transactions execute concurrently, the system guarantees that for every pair of transactions T_i and T_j, it appears to T_i that either T_j finished execution before T_i started, or T_j started execution after T_i finished. 4. Durability: Once a transaction successfully commits, the updates made to the database persist even in the event of system crashes.

OSI Reference Model vs TCP/IP Protocol Stack The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) reference model, developed by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), is a conceptual framework with seven distinct architectural layers: 1. Physical Layer: Transmission and reception of raw unstructured bit streams over physical media. 2. Data Link Layer: Node-to-node frame transfer, media access control (MAC), and error detection (CRC). 3. Network Layer: Multi-hop routing, packet forwarding, and logical addressing (IPv4, IPv6). 4. Transport Layer: End-to-end process-to-process communication, multiplexing (TCP, UDP). 5. Session Layer: Dialog control, token management, and synchronization checkpoints. 6. Presentation Layer: Syntax translation, character encoding, data compression, and encryption/SSL. 7. Application Layer: High-level network application services (HTTP, DNS, SMTP, FTP). In contrast, the practical TCP/IP Internet model consolidates the top three layers into a single Application Layer, resulting in a streamlined four-layer stack: Network Interface (Link), Internet (IP), Transport (TCP/UDP), and Application.

Two-Phase Locking (2PL) and Serializability Serializability is the standard criterion for the correctness of concurrent transaction execution. A concurrent schedule is conflict serializable if it is conflict equivalent to some serial schedule, which can be verified by constructing a precedence (or serialization) graph: a schedule is conflict serializable if and only if its precedence graph has no directed cycles. The Two-Phase Locking (2PL) protocol is a concurrency control mechanism that guarantees conflict serializability. Under basic 2PL: - Growing Phase: A transaction may acquire locks (shared or exclusive), but cannot release any lock. - Shrinking Phase: A transaction may release locks, but cannot acquire any new lock. Strict 2PL further requires that all exclusive locks held by a transaction be released only after the transaction commits or aborts, which prevents cascading rollbacks. Rigorous 2PL requires both shared and exclusive locks to be held until commit.

Computer Networks: Transport Layer Protocols and TCP 3-Way Handshake The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) is a connection-oriented, reliable, byte-stream transport layer protocol defined in RFC 793. Unlike UDP, which is connectionless and best-effort, TCP provides guaranteed in-order delivery, flow control, and congestion control. Before data transfer begins, TCP establishes a virtual connection between client and server using a Three-Way Handshake: 1. SYN: The active client generates a randomly chosen Initial Sequence Number (ISN_client = x) and sends a TCP segment with the SYN control flag set to 1. 2. SYN-ACK: The passive server receives the SYN segment, allocates connection buffers and state variables, generates its own Initial Sequence Number (ISN_server = y), and transmits a segment with SYN=1 and ACK=1, where the acknowledgment number is set to x + 1. 3. ACK: The client receives the SYN-ACK, transitions to the ESTABLISHED state, and transmits an ACK segment with ACK=1 and acknowledgment number set to y + 1. Data payloads can accompany this third packet.

Theory of Computation: Finite Automata and Regular Languages A Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA) is formally defined as a 5-tuple (Q, Sigma, delta, q_0, F), where Q is a finite set of states, Sigma is a finite alphabet of input symbols, delta is the transition function mapping Q x Sigma to Q, q_0 in Q is the initial start state, and F subset of Q is the set of accept (or final) states. DFAs recognize the class of regular languages. A Non-Deterministic Finite Automaton (NFA) differs in its transition function, which maps Q x (Sigma union {epsilon}) to the power set 2^Q, allowing state transitions on empty strings (epsilon transitions) or multiple possible subsequent states for a single symbol. Despite this flexibility, the subset construction algorithm proves that NFAs and DFAs have equivalent computational power: any NFA with n states can be converted to an equivalent DFA with at most 2^n states.
